title: CS161 15 - Network Basics, ARP, DHCP and WPA

questions.q: Which layer uses the physical layer as a building block to connect local machines into a LAN?
choices: Layer 1 (Physical)
Layer 2 (Link)
Layer 3 (Internetwork)
Layer 4 (Transport)
questions.explain: Layer 1 moves bits across space; layer 2 (link) uses it to connect local machines in a LAN; layer 3 connects many LANs.

questions.q: What is a router?
choices: A machine connected to two or more LANs that forwards messages from one LAN to another
A simple repeater that rebroadcasts every packet to all of its outputs
A server that hands out IP addresses to new machines
A device that translates IP addresses into MAC addresses
questions.explain: A router connects multiple LANs. In the postal analogy it is the post office that forwards your letter to another apartment complex.

questions.q: In the layered Internet model, what layer number is the Transport layer?
questions.explain: 1 Physical, 2 Link, 3 (Inter)Network, 4 Transport, 5 and 6 obsolete, 6.5 Secure Transport, 7 Application.

questions.q: Which layer was added to the model at position 6.5?
choices: Application
Secure Transport
Session
Presentation
questions.explain: Layers 5 and 6 are obsolete, and a Secure Transport layer (6.5) was added for security.

questions.q: If a network switches from wired to wireless communication at layer 1, the protocols at the higher layers must change too.
questions.explain: Layering gives a clean abstraction barrier. The layer 1 implementation does not affect protocols at the other layers.

questions.q: In what order do the parts of a packet appear, from the start of the packet?
choices: Link header, IP header, transport header, application data
Application data, transport header, IP header, link header
IP header, link header, transport header, application data
Transport header, IP header, link header, application data
questions.explain: Each layer adds its header in front of what the layer above gave it, so the lowest layer's header ends up first.

questions.q: When a message arrives, it moves up the protocol stack starting at the lowest layer, and each layer removes its own header before passing the rest to the layer above.
questions.explain: Unpacking is the reverse of sending. When the message reaches the highest layer, every header has been processed.

questions.q: What does a network protocol specify?
choices: How communication is structured (e.g., message format)
How machines behave while communicating (e.g., actions needed to send and receive)
How errors are handled (e.g., a message timing out)
Which physical medium (wire or radio) every network must use
questions.explain: A protocol is an agreement on message structure, behavior and error handling. The physical medium is a separate layer 1 choice.

questions.q: In the postal analogy, what does a packet header correspond to?
choices: The letter itself
The envelope
The post office
The apartment complex
questions.explain: A header comes before the data and holds delivery metadata such as sender, recipient and length, like an envelope.

questions.q: How many bits long is a MAC address?
questions.explain: MAC addresses are 48 bits (6 bytes), written as 6 hex pairs such as ca:fe:f0:0d:be:ef.

questions.q: How many bits long is an IPv4 address?
questions.explain: IPv4 addresses are 32 bits (4 bytes), written as 4 integers from 0 to 255, such as 128.32.131.10.

questions.q: How many bits long is a port number?
questions.explain: Higher layers give each process on a machine a unique 16-bit port number.

questions.q: How many bits long is an IPv6 address?
questions.explain: IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses, written as 8 two-byte hex values separated by colons.

questions.q: What is the broadcast MAC address, which means "send this to everyone on the local network"?
questions.explain: ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff is the special broadcast MAC address.

questions.q: Which kind of address is like an apartment number: unique inside one local network but useless for identifying one machine worldwide?
choices: MAC address
IP address
Port number
SSID
questions.explain: MAC addresses identify machines on a LAN (layer 2). IP addresses (layer 3) identify machines globally.

questions.q: Why do higher layers use port numbers?
choices: So that several processes on one machine can each communicate over the network
So that a machine can be identified globally
So that machines on the same LAN can be told apart
So that packets can be encrypted
questions.explain: A machine has one IP address but may have many tabs and applications using the network. Ports tell those processes apart, like room numbers in a building.

questions.q: Which addresses are in the layer 3 header?
choices: MAC addresses
IP addresses
Port numbers
SSIDs
questions.explain: The layer 2 header holds MAC addresses, the layer 3 header holds IP addresses, and higher layer headers hold port numbers.

questions.q: In networking, cryptographic message authentication codes are sometimes called MICs (message integrity codes) so they are not confused with MAC addresses.
questions.explain: MAC can mean a hardware address or a message authentication code. MIC is the name used for the cryptographic one in networking.

questions.q: IP (layer 3) guarantees that every packet arrives uncorrupted.
questions.explain: IP only offers best-effort delivery and does not handle errors. Packets can be corrupted or lost, and higher layers provide correctness and security.

questions.q: At the physical, link and internetwork layers, the network keeps track of connections between pairs of hosts.
questions.explain: These layers have no concept of a connection. Each packet is handled on its own, and higher layers build two-way connections out of packets.

questions.q: Which type of network adversary can read packets on a connection but cannot modify them?
choices: Off-path
On-path
In-path
Man-in-the-middle
questions.explain: Off-path: can't read or modify. On-path: can read but not modify. In-path (man-in-the-middle): can read, modify and block.

questions.q: Which list orders network adversaries from weakest to strongest?
choices: Off-path, on-path, in-path
On-path, off-path, in-path
In-path, on-path, off-path
Off-path, in-path, on-path
questions.explain: Off-path sees nothing, on-path can read, and in-path can read, modify and block.

questions.q: What is another name for an in-path adversary?
choices: Sniffer
Man-in-the-middle
Spoofer
Off-path attacker
questions.explain: An in-path adversary can read, modify and block packets, which makes it a man-in-the-middle.

questions.q: Which adversaries can send their own packets with spoofed headers?
choices: Off-path adversaries
On-path adversaries
In-path adversaries
questions.explain: Every adversary can send packets, including spoofed ones. Often it is as simple as setting the source field to someone else's address.

questions.q: What does ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) do?
choices: Translates IP addresses into MAC addresses
Translates MAC addresses into IP addresses
Translates host names into IP addresses
Assigns IP addresses to new machines
questions.explain: ARP is a link layer (2) protocol that maps a layer 3 IP address to a layer 2 MAC address.

questions.q: Alice knows Bob's IP is 1.1.1.1 and needs his MAC address. What is the first step of ARP?
choices: Alice broadcasts to the LAN: "What is the MAC address of 1.1.1.1?"
Alice sends a request directly to Bob's MAC address
Alice asks the DHCP server for Bob's MAC address
Alice checks with the switch's VLAN table
questions.explain: Alice broadcasts the request. Bob replies only to Alice with his IP and MAC, and Alice caches the mapping.

questions.q: During ARP, who replies if the requested IP address belongs to a machine outside the LAN?
choices: The router, with its own MAC address
The remote machine, with its own MAC address
Nobody, because ARP only works inside the LAN
The DNS server
questions.explain: For off-LAN destinations, the router answers with its MAC so the traffic goes to the router for forwarding.

questions.q: A machine caches an ARP reply only if it sent a matching broadcast request first.
questions.explain: Received ARP replies are always cached, even if no request was ever made.

questions.q: Mallory sends Alice a spoofed ARP reply that maps Bob's IP to Mallory's MAC, and it arrives before Bob's real reply. What kind of adversary is Mallory now?
choices: Off-path
On-path only
Man-in-the-middle
None, because the attack fails
questions.explain: Alice's traffic for Bob now goes to Mallory, who can read and modify it before forwarding it to Bob.

questions.q: Why is ARP spoofing called a race condition?
choices: The on-path attacker can't block the real reply, so the forged reply has to arrive first
The attacker has to brute-force the MAC address before the cache entry expires
Two switches compete to forward the same packet
The victim's cache can hold only one entry at a time
questions.explain: On-path attackers can't stop the legitimate response, so their own response must win the race to fool the victim.

questions.q: On a broadcast Ethernet network such as one built on a hub, what kind of adversary is someone on the same LAN as the victim?
choices: Off-path
On-path
In-path
None
questions.explain: They can see all traffic and inject spoofed packets, but they can't block or modify packets in transit, so they are on-path.

questions.q: What is the Ethernet device mode called in which the device receives all packets, not just those addressed to it or to broadcast?
questions.explain: In promiscuous mode a device sniffs every packet. Ignoring other machines' packets is enforced only in software.

questions.q: On broadcast Ethernet, receivers are prevented from reading packets meant for other machines by a hardware restriction.
questions.explain: Receivers are only supposed to ignore those packets, and that is enforced in software. Promiscuous mode lets a device receive everything.

questions.q: What is a network hub?
choices: A simple repeater that rebroadcasts every packet it receives to all outputs
A device that sends a packet only to the MAC that the cache lists for its IP
A device that splits a network into isolated virtual networks
A device connecting two or more LANs
questions.explain: A hub broadcasts everything, so every node sees all traffic. Switches forward based on a cache.

questions.q: Which of these defend against ARP spoofing on a wired LAN?
choices: Using switches instead of hubs
Running a tool like arpwatch to monitor IP-to-MAC pairings for suspicious changes
Switching the network to WPA2-Enterprise
Making all ARP replies broadcast instead of sent to one machine
questions.explain: Switches and arpwatch are the defenses. WPA2-Enterprise is still vulnerable to an authenticated user running an ARP attack.

questions.q: What does a switch do with a packet whose IP address has no known MAC in its cache?
choices: Broadcasts it to everyone
Drops it
Sends it back to the sender
Forwards it to the DHCP server
questions.explain: With a known MAC, the switch sends the packet only to that MAC. Otherwise it broadcasts. Smarter switches can filter requests so they aren't all broadcast.

questions.q: What do VLANs (Virtual Local Area Networks) on better switches provide?
choices: Isolation, by splitting the network into separate virtual networks
Encryption of every link layer frame
Automatic IP address assignment
Translation of private IP addresses into public ones
questions.explain: VLANs isolate traffic by dividing one physical network into separate virtual networks.

questions.q: What is the correct order of the DHCP handshake?
choices: Client Discover, Server Offer, Client Request, Server Acknowledge
Server Offer, Client Discover, Client Request, Server Acknowledge
Client Request, Server Offer, Client Discover, Server Acknowledge
Client Discover, Client Request, Server Offer, Server Acknowledge
questions.explain: The client asks for a configuration, servers offer one, the client broadcasts its choice, and the chosen server confirms.

questions.q: Which items does a machine get from DHCP when it joins a network?
choices: Its own IP address
The IP address of the DNS server
The IP address of the router (gateway)
The WiFi password
The MAC addresses of every machine on the LAN
questions.explain: You need an IP so others can reach you, the DNS server's IP to resolve names, and the gateway's IP to reach the Internet.

questions.q: What is another name for the router's IP address that DHCP gives a client so it can reach the Internet?
questions.explain: The router is also called the gateway.

questions.q: Which DHCP messages are broadcast?
choices: Client Discover
Server Offer
Client Request
Server Acknowledge
questions.explain: Both client messages are broadcast.

questions.q: Why must the DHCP Client Discover message be broadcast?
choices: Before DHCP, the client doesn't know where the servers are
So every server knows which offer was chosen
To stop attackers from forging offers
Because the client already has a gateway address
questions.explain: The client has no configuration yet, so it can't address any particular server.

questions.q: Why must the DHCP Client Request message be broadcast?
choices: So that if several servers made offers, they all learn which one was chosen
Because the client doesn't yet know any server's address
So that the switch can update its MAC cache
To encrypt the chosen configuration
questions.explain: Broadcasting the choice tells every server that made an offer which one was accepted.

questions.q: What happens when a DHCP lease time runs out?
choices: The client must ask to renew the lease, or the server frees those settings for other devices
The client keeps the configuration permanently
The router switches the client to IPv6
The client must redo the WPA2 handshake
questions.explain: The lease (the configuration from the server offer) can carry a lease time. Once it expires the client must renew or lose the settings.

questions.q: Why is DHCP sometimes called a layer 2-3 protocol?
choices: It sets up the configuration that allows communication over LANs and the Internet, so it doesn't fit cleanly into one layer
It carries both MAC addresses and port numbers in its header
It runs on routers, which sit between layers 2 and 3
It encrypts traffic at both layers
questions.explain: The layers are defined mainly for communication. Setup protocols like DHCP don't fit neatly inside the abstraction barriers.

questions.q: With NAT, a computer on the local network sends a packet to the Internet. Which address does the router replace?
choices: The source IP address (the placeholder becomes a valid IP)
The destination IP address
The destination port only
The destination MAC address only
questions.explain: For an outgoing packet the router swaps the private placeholder source IP for a valid one. For replies it converts the destination back to the placeholder.

questions.q: NAT placeholder addresses usually come from a reserved block of private IP addresses that are not valid on the Internet.
questions.explain: Private addresses work as placeholders inside the local network, and the router translates them so many computers can share one valid IP.

questions.q: Why does NAT exist?
choices: There are more computers than IPv4 addresses, so several computers need to share one IP address
To encrypt traffic leaving the local network
To turn MAC addresses into IP addresses
To stop DHCP spoofing
questions.explain: IPv4 address space is too small and not every network supports IPv6, so NAT lets a local network share an address.

questions.q: An attacker wins the race with a forged DHCP offer. Which forged values let the attacker become a man-in-the-middle?
choices: Their own IP address as the gateway address
Their own IP address as the DNS server address
A longer lease time
The broadcast MAC address as the client's MAC
questions.explain: A forged gateway sends the victim's outbound packets to the attacker. A forged DNS server lets the attacker give malicious name-to-IP translations.

questions.q: How do many networks deal with DHCP spoofing in practice?
choices: They accept it as a fact of life and rely on higher layers, such as encryption, for protection
They use switches with VLANs to block all forged offers
They require WPA2-PSK on every wired port
They sign every DHCP offer with a certificate the client already trusts
questions.explain: If messages are properly encrypted at higher layers, a man-in-the-middle can't do much with them.

questions.q: Why is it hard to defend against low-layer attacks like DHCP spoofing?
choices: No trusted party exists to rely on when a machine first joins the network
DHCP messages are too short to carry a MAC
DHCP runs only over wireless links
Routers can't see DHCP traffic
questions.explain: When a machine first connects, it has no established trust or keys to check whether an offer is legitimate.

questions.q: How is the attack on DHCP similar to ARP spoofing?
choices: An on-path attacker sees a broadcast request and races to send a forged reply before the legitimate one
Both require the attacker to know the WiFi password
Both work by brute-forcing a low-entropy password
Both need the attacker to physically block the legitimate server
questions.explain: In both, the attacker sees the request and wins a race with a spoofed response. The victim accepts whichever arrives first.

questions.q: What is the name of the WiFi network that an access point announces in its beacon packets?
questions.explain: The AP keeps broadcasting beacons that say "I am here" and give the network name, the SSID.

questions.q: On a WiFi network with no password, data is sent unencrypted, so others on the network can see your traffic and inject packets.
questions.explain: Without WPA2 there is no encryption, and attacks like ARP spoofing work as they do on a wired LAN.

questions.q: In WPA2-PSK, how is the PSK (Pre-Shared Key) derived?
choices: PBKDF2-SHA1 applied to the SSID and the WiFi password
SHA1 applied to the AP's MAC address
From the ANonce and SNonce
Picked at random by an authentication server
questions.explain: Both the AP and the client run a slow password-based key derivation function over the SSID and password.

questions.q: Why is the SSID an input to the PSK derivation?
choices: So two networks with the same password still get different PSKs
So the PSK changes every handshake
So each user on the network gets a unique key
So the access point can be authenticated by TLS
questions.explain: The SSID acts somewhat like a salt, so the same password on different networks gives different PSKs.

questions.q: Why is a slow password-based key derivation function (PBKDF2) used to make the PSK?
choices: It makes brute-forcing the password harder
It makes the handshake shorter
It hides the nonces from eavesdroppers
It makes the PSK unique for each user
questions.explain: Password-based KDFs are slower by a large constant factor, which raises the cost of each password guess.

questions.q: Once the client and AP both have the PSK, why don't they just use the PSK to encrypt everything?
choices: Everyone on the network has the same PSK, so other users could decrypt your traffic
The PSK is too short to be an encryption key
The PSK is sent in the clear during the handshake
The PSK expires after one message
questions.explain: The handshake gives each client its own keys (the PTK), so other users can't simply decrypt everything with the shared PSK.

questions.q: Which values go into deriving the PTK (Pairwise Transport Keys) in WPA2-PSK?
choices: The ANonce
The SNonce
The PSK
The MAC addresses of the access point and the client
The GTK
The client's DHCP-assigned IP address
questions.explain: PTK = f(ANonce, SNonce, PSK, AP MAC, client MAC). The GTK is sent encrypted after the PTK is derived.

questions.q: What do the random ANonce and SNonce do in the WPA2 handshake?
choices: They make each handshake produce different keys
They encrypt the GTK
They identify the network by name
They prove the client knows the username and password
questions.explain: Fresh nonces give fresh keys on every handshake. They are sent without encryption.

questions.q: Why do the client and AP exchange MICs during the WPA2 handshake?
choices: To check that nobody tampered with the nonces and that both sides derived the same PTK
To send the GTK
To agree on an IP address
To announce the SSID
questions.explain: The MICs are cryptographic MACs keyed from the PTK, so they confirm integrity and that both sides derived the same keys.

questions.q: What is the GTK (Group Temporal Key) used for?
choices: Encrypting and decrypting broadcast messages sent to ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff
Encrypting one client's traffic with the AP
Deriving the PSK from the password
Authenticating to the WPA2-Enterprise server
questions.explain: Everyone on the network shares the GTK, so all clients can send and receive broadcast messages. Unicast traffic uses the PTK.

questions.q: Each client on a WPA2 network gets its own unique GTK.
questions.explain: The GTK is the same for everyone, which is what lets everyone handle broadcast messages. The PTK is the per-client key.

questions.q: How many messages does the optimized WPA2 handshake used in practice exchange?
questions.explain: The 4-way handshake: ANonce; SNonce + MIC; encrypted GTK + MIC; ACK.

questions.q: In the optimized 4-way handshake, what does the client send in message 2?
choices: The SNonce and a MIC, after deriving the PTK from the ANonce
The ANonce
The encrypted GTK and a MIC
An ACK confirming receipt of the GTK
questions.explain: Once it has the ANonce, the client has everything it needs, so it derives the PTK and then sends the SNonce with a MIC. Message 3 is the AP's encrypted GTK + MIC.

questions.q: Which part of the WPA2 handshake is sent encrypted?
choices: Only the GTK
The nonces
The MICs
Everything
questions.explain: Everything except the GTK is sent in the clear, which is why eavesdroppers can collect the nonces and MAC addresses.

questions.q: An attacker who knows the WiFi password records another user's entire WPA2-PSK handshake. What can the attacker do?
choices: Derive that user's PTK, then decrypt their traffic and encrypt and inject messages
Only read broadcast messages
Nothing, because the PTK is unique to each client
Only learn the user's MAC address
questions.explain: The attacker has the PSK from the password, and the nonces and MACs travel in the clear, so they have every input to the PTK.

questions.q: An attacker who does NOT know the WiFi password records a WPA2-PSK handshake. How can they still recover the PTK?
choices: Guess passwords offline: derive PSK and then PTK for each guess, and check it against the recorded MICs
Read the PTK, since it is sent in the clear
Decrypt the GTK with the ANonce
Send a spoofed ARP reply to the access point
questions.explain: The MICs let the attacker check each guess. A low-entropy password can be brute-forced with enough computing power.

questions.q: What is the root problem behind the WPA2-PSK attacks?
choices: Every user derives their keys from the same secret, the shared WiFi password
The nonces are too short
The GTK is sent unencrypted
PBKDF2 is too fast
questions.explain: Anyone with the shared password can derive the PSK. The fix is to give each user a unique source of secrecy.

questions.q: In WPA2-Enterprise, what takes the place of the PSK when deriving the PTK?
choices: A random PMK (Pairwise Master Key) that an authentication server gives to both the client and the AP
A hash of the user's username
The GTK
The SSID alone
questions.explain: After the user proves their identity with a unique username and password over TLS, the server sends a per-user random PMK. The handshake then runs as before with the PMK.

questions.q: How does a client prove its identity in WPA2-Enterprise before the handshake?
choices: It gives its own username and password to an authentication server over a TLS-secured connection
It types in the shared WiFi password
It sends its MAC address to the AP
It broadcasts a DHCP Discover message
questions.explain: Each authorized user has a unique username and password, checked by a secure authentication server.

questions.q: WPA2-Enterprise stops another authenticated user on the same network from becoming a man-in-the-middle with ARP or DHCP spoofing.
questions.explain: WPA2-Enterprise defeats the handshake-eavesdropping and password brute-force attacks, but an authenticated user can still run ARP or DHCP attacks.
